figures.alt: Line chart showing the foreign-born share of the U.S. population rising from 4.7 percent in 1970 to 13.6 percent in 2020
figures.caption: Share of the U.S. population that was foreign-born, 1970-2020. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, decennial censuses.
figures.license: Chart data: public U.S. government data

books.section: Topic 9.5 Migration and Immigration in the 1990s and 2000s
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)

options.misconception: The chart shows a steady decline in immigration after 1970.
options.text: A steady decline in immigration to the United States after 1970

options.misconception: The chart shows the end of all European immigration by 1970.
options.text: The end of all immigration from Europe by 1970

options.misconception: The chart shows a decline in the total U.S. population.
options.text: A decline in the total U.S. population after 1970
An increase in immigration after 1965, especially from Latin America and Asia

rationales.A: The share rose; immigration did not decline steadily.
rationales.B: European immigration did not end by 1970.
rationales.C: The total population grew; the chart shows a rising share, not a falling total.
rationales.D: The foreign-born share more than doubled from 1970 to 2020, reflecting rising immigration, especially from Latin America and Asia. The rise was steady at every census, not a single spike, and it followed the 1965 opening of immigration.
rationales.general:
1. Read the trend. The foreign-born share rises at every step, from 4.7 percent to 13.6 percent.
2. Ask what a rising share means. More of the population was born abroad, reflecting rising immigration.
3. Test the misreadings. The trend is up, not down; European immigration did not end; and a share is not a total.
4. Match the reflection. Rising immigration after 1965, especially from Latin America and Asia.
Remember: read a share as a share. A rising line means a growing part of the whole.
